title: The Lumières' 1895 Paris screening
description: On December 28, 1895, the Lumières projected short everyday-life films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris, usually counted as cinema's birth; their light three-in-one Cinématographe traveled the world.

facts.text: The Lumières' first films recorded everyday French life, such as workers leaving the Lumière factory and a train arriving at a station.

title: The Great Train Robbery tells a story across places
description: Porter's 1903 film for Edison's company used 14 shots and cut between the telegraph operator and the bandits to show simultaneous action, a break from theater-like staging.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery (1903) was made by Edwin S. Porter for Thomas Edison's company and runs about 12 minutes.
Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train to show action happening at the same time in different places.

title: The nickelodeon boom
description: Cheap storefront theaters, named for their nickel admission, spread from Pittsburgh in 1905 to thousands by 1908 and made movies everyday entertainment.

facts.text: A nickelodeon was an early movie theater named for its nickel admission; it showed short films continuously, with piano accompaniment.
Harry Davis's Pittsburgh nickelodeon, opened in 1905, became the model for the rapid spread of nickelodeons across the United States.
Nickelodeons were makeshift theaters in converted storefronts, showing about an hour's worth of films for 5 to 10 cents.
Britannica credits the popularity of The Great Train Robbery with encouraging investors and leading to the first permanent film theaters, the nickelodeons.
The number of nickelodeons in the United States grew from a handful in 1904 to between 8,000 and 10,000 by 1908.
Nickelodeons were first identified with working-class audiences, drew more middle-class viewers as the decade went on, and became tied to the rising popularity of the story film.

title: Film exchanges: renting instead of buying
description: Instead of buying prints outright, theaters rented them from film exchanges, which bought prints from producers and leased them cheaply.

facts.text: From about 1897 producers sold film prints outright to exhibitors.
Around 1903 Harry and Herbert Miles opened a film exchange in San Francisco that bought prints from producers and leased them to exhibitors for 25 percent of the purchase price.

title: The Trust: the Motion Picture Patents Company
description: In 1908 leading film companies, Edison's among them, pooled their patents in the Motion Picture Patents Company and licensed who could make and show films.

facts.text: In 1908 leading film companies, including Edison's and Biograph, formed the Motion Picture Patents Company, known as the Trust, pooling the key US film patents.
The Trust licensed its patents only to approved companies and had an exclusive deal with Eastman Kodak, so raw film stock went only to licensed producers.
The US government sued the Motion Picture Patents Company under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and the company was formally dissolved in 1918.

title: Why filmmaking moved to Hollywood
description: Southern California offered year-round sun, varied scenery and cheap land and labor, and distance from the Trust is generally thought to have helped; by 1915 Hollywood was the center of US filmmaking.

facts.text: In 1911 a site on Sunset Boulevard became Hollywood's first studio, and soon about 20 companies were producing films in the area.
By 1915 Hollywood had become the center of the American film industry as independent filmmakers moved there from the East Coast, with more than 60 percent of American production based there.
Southern California offered a temperate climate for year-round filming, a wide range of scenery within 50 miles of Hollywood, low taxes, and cheap, plentiful labor and land.
It is generally thought that Hollywood's distance from the Motion Picture Patents Company's headquarters in New York City made it attractive to independent filmmakers.

title: Alice Guy's early story films
description: Alice Guy, Léon Gaumont's secretary, directed La Fée aux choux, one of the first films to tell a made-up story, and went on to run Gaumont's production.

facts.text: Hired as Léon Gaumont's secretary, Alice Guy directed her first film, La Fée aux choux (The Cabbage Fairy), which Britannica dates to 1896; a few historians date it as late as 1900.
Britannica says Guy is generally acknowledged to be the first director to film a narrative story, and many historians hold that her fairy tale preceded Méliès's story films.
Guy became the Gaumont company's head of production, directing nearly all Gaumont films made until 1905.
From 1906 to 1907 Guy directed short sound films using Gaumont's Chronophone.

title: Alice Guy's American studio and lost credit
description: Guy moved to the United States in 1907, founded Solax in 1910 and built a Fort Lee studio, yet many of her achievements were later forgotten or credited to men.

facts.text: In 1907 Guy married cameraman Herbert Blaché and moved to the United States, where in 1910 she founded the Solax Company.
By 1912 Solax had a new, state-of-the-art studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey.
Many of Guy's accomplishments were forgotten or credited to male colleagues, and after returning to France in 1922 she could not find work in its film industry.

title: Griffith's techniques and the feature film
description: D. W. Griffith refined the close-up and cross-cutting over hundreds of Biograph shorts, and his nearly three-hour The Birth of a Nation secured the feature-length film.

facts.text: From 1908 to 1913 D. W. Griffith made more than 400 films for Biograph, mostly one-reelers.
Britannica says Griffith introduced or refined techniques of film storytelling, including the close-up and cross-cutting, which edits together scenes at different locations.
The Birth of a Nation (1915), based on Thomas Dixon's 1905 novel The Clansman, ran nearly three hours, the longest film released up to that time.
The Birth of a Nation used special effects, jump cuts and facial close-ups, and Britannica says it secured the future of feature-length films and the acceptance of film as a serious medium.

title: The racism of The Birth of a Nation and the protests against it
description: The Birth of a Nation portrayed Black people as unworthy of freedom and glorified the Ku Klux Klan; the NAACP led protests, and the film inspired the Klan's 1915 revival.

facts.text: The Birth of a Nation portrays Black people during Reconstruction as unworthy of freedom and voting rights, and shows the Ku Klux Klan as heroes restoring order.
In The Birth of a Nation, Black characters such as Gus were played by white actors in blackface.
Protests, mainly organized by the NAACP, met The Birth of a Nation from its 1915 premiere, and showings were stopped in a few states and cities.
In late 1915 the Ku Klux Klan was revived in Georgia, directly inspired by The Birth of a Nation.
Griffith responded to criticism of The Birth of a Nation with Intolerance (1916), a film about intolerance and censorship.

title: Chaplin's Tramp
description: Charlie Chaplin's Tramp, first seen in 1914, mixed physical comedy with poignancy; Chaplin directed his own films and cofounded United Artists.

facts.text: While touring America with the Karno company in 1913, Charlie Chaplin was signed to appear in Mack Sennett's Keystone comedies.
Chaplin's Tramp first appeared in Kid Auto Races at Venice (1914), wearing a too-small coat, too-large pants, floppy shoes and a battered derby, with a small mustache and a cane.
Chaplin blended physical comedy with poignancy; in The Gold Rush (1925) the Tramp must eat his shoe to stay alive.
Chaplin became his own director, and in 1919 he cofounded United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith.

title: Keaton's deadpan stunts
description: Buster Keaton, the Great Stone Face, did dangerous stunts with an unsmiling face, timed to the inch, as in the falling house front of Steamboat Bill, Jr.

facts.text: In Steamboat Bill, Jr. (1928), a house front falls on Buster Keaton, who survives by standing on a nail-marked spot where its open attic window lands; had he moved, he would have been crushed.
Keaton grew up in his family's vaudeville act, the Three Keatons, known for knockabout acrobatics, and learned to take pratfalls without injury.
Buster Keaton, known as the Great Stone Face, performed death-defying stunts while keeping an unsmiling expression.
Keaton said that the more serious he turned, the bigger the laugh he could get.
In The General, a Civil War comedy, Keaton staged most of the action and stunts in and around trains.

title: Intertitles
description: Silent films cut to printed cards, intertitles, for dialogue or explanation; a few films, like The Last Laugh, managed almost without them.

facts.text: Silent films used printed intertitles for dialogue or explanation.
F. W. Murnau's Der letzte Mann (The Last Laugh, 1924) told its story almost entirely without printed intertitles.

title: Live music at the silent movies
description: Silent films were almost always shown with live music: an improvising pianist at first, organs and orchestras in big theaters, guided by cue sheets and compiled scores.

facts.text: Silent films were almost always shown with live music: early screenings usually had a solo pianist, often improvising, and larger theaters used organists or orchestras.
Films were eventually distributed with published cue sheets suggesting what the pianist or organist should play.
The Birth of a Nation was shown with an orchestra playing Joseph Carl Breil's score, a compilation drawn from many sources.

title: Movie palaces
description: From 1914, huge, luxurious 'dream palaces' such as New York's Strand gave films grand theaters with thousands of seats.

facts.text: New York's Strand Theatre, opened in 1914, was the first of the 'dream palaces', huge movie theaters with luxurious interiors, and seated around 3,000 people.

title: Caligari's sets show a state of mind
description: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari used distorted sets and painted light and shadow to show a narrator's tortured mind.

facts.text: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, directed by Robert Wiene in postwar Germany, tells of murders committed by a sleepwalker at the bidding of a demented showman.
To represent the narrator's tortured state of mind, Wiene hired three Expressionist artists to design sets with exaggerated dimensions and deformed spatial relationships.
Patterns of light and shadow were painted directly onto Caligari's scenery and even the characters' makeup, partly to save electric power, which was rationed in postwar Germany.

title: German Expressionism
description: Caligari's success gave rise to German Expressionism, a movement of stylized, shadowy films including Murnau's Nosferatu.

facts.text: By embodying disturbed psychological states through décor, Caligari greatly influenced the UFA films that followed and gave rise to the movement known as German Expressionism.
F. W. Murnau directed one of the movement's classics, Nosferatu (1922), an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's novel Dracula.

title: Soviet cinema learns to edit
description: Lenin's government made film a priority and founded the world's first film school; short of film stock, teachers such as Kuleshov studied how Griffith's shots were assembled.

facts.text: Lenin recognized film's importance as propaganda and its power to communicate quickly, and his government gave top priority to developing the Soviet film industry.
The Soviet state film school in Moscow, later known as VGIK, was the first film school in the world.
A foreign blockade stopped the Soviet Union importing film equipment and stock, which it could not yet make itself, and power shortages limited what remained.
Teacher Lev Kuleshov screened a print of Griffith's Intolerance for his workshop students until they had memorized its shot structures.
Soviet filmmakers held that time and space in film must be subordinate to editing, which they called montage, from the French verb monter, 'to assemble'.

title: Eisenstein's montage of collision
description: Sergei Eisenstein held that meaning comes from the collision of opposing shots, and put the idea to work in the Odessa Steps sequence of Battleship Potemkin (1925).

facts.text: Eisenstein believed that meaning in film is generated by the collision of opposing shots, producing a new idea, and compared the process to the explosions of an internal combustion engine.
Battleship Potemkin (1925), commissioned for the 20th anniversary of the 1905 Revolution, dramatizes a mutiny by the sailors of the battleship Potemkin.
Potemkin's 'Odessa Steps' sequence, in which soldiers massacre citizens on a stone staircase, is one of the most famous sequences in film history, and montage gives the slaughter symbolic meaning.

title: What Nanook of the North staged
description: Nanook of the North filmed real Inuit people and skills, but arranged much for the camera: a cut-away igloo, a staged seal hunt, a borrowed family and harpoons instead of rifles.

facts.text: Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922), a dramatic interpretation of Inuit life in the Canadian Arctic, was an international success.
Flaherty arrived at Port Harrison (now Inukjuak) in northern Quebec in August 1920 to shoot the film; Allakariallak, chosen as the best hunter in the district, played Nanook.
To film inside an igloo, a second igloo was built with a wall removed to make room for the camera and its operator.
The two women shown as Nanook's wives were not his wives, and the two children were not his.
Nanook's famous seal hunt was staged, as close viewing of the cuts shows.
By 1920 Inuit hunters used rifles, but Flaherty had his subjects hunt with harpoons and spears to show an older way of life.

title: Flaherty and the word documentary
description: Flaherty is often called the father of the documentary film, and John Grierson first used the word documentary about Flaherty's Moana (1926).

facts.text: Robert Flaherty is often called the father of the documentary film.
John Grierson first used the term documentary in a reference to Flaherty's film Moana (1926).

title: Most American silent features are lost
description: A 2013 Library of Congress study found only 14 percent of 1912-1929 US features survive complete in their original form; nitrate decay, fire and neglect after sound destroyed most of the rest.

facts.text: A 2013 study by historian David Pierce for the Library of Congress found that only 14 percent of US feature films from 1912 to 1929 survive complete on 35mm as released; another 11 percent survive in foreign versions or lesser formats.
Derived from the 2013 study: with 14 percent of 1912-1929 US features surviving in original form and 11 percent in other versions, about three in four are lost.
The losses are blamed on nitrate film's vulnerability to fire and decay and the film industry's practice of neglecting or destroying prints and negatives.
Silent feature films disappeared from sight soon after the coming of sound, and many vanished from existence.
